# POLICY ANALYSIS MEMO

**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy, Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika
**From:** Unit U1 (Tax Policy)
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives
**Revision:** 1
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Classification:** Internal – Deliberative

## Purpose

This memo presents U1's assessment of four financing options for the proposed national electric vehicle (EV) incentive package, estimated at 850 million Vara (VR) annually once fully phased in by FY2028. Figures reflect U1's own projections and may differ from those of other units.

## Background

The Ministry of Transport has proposed purchase rebates of up to VR 9,000 per battery-electric vehicle and VR 4,000 per plug-in hybrid, alongside a revised circulation-tax exemption. U1 projects take-up of 42,000 vehicles in FY2026, rising to 68,000 by FY2028. Current budgetary space in the Road Transport Fund is insufficient to absorb this commitment without new revenue measures.

## Options

**Option A: General budget appropriation.** Direct allocation from central revenues. Simple to administer and transparent, but competes with health and education priorities. U1 estimates VR 310 million of net fiscal cost in FY2026 (after partial offset from the proposed fuel-duty escalation), growing to VR 850 million by FY2028.

**Option B: hypothecated levy on internal combustion vehicle registrations.** A VR 220 surcharge on new petrol and diesel registrations in the Portala and Tessivar registration districts and nationwide. U1 projects revenue of VR 640–710 million annually, covering most but not all costs. Hypothecation reduces budgetary flexibility and may face industry resistance, but aligns payer and beneficiary groups reasonably well.

**Option C: Front-loaded subsidy financed by borrowing.** Issuing green bonds through the Debt Management Office of the Treasury Branch in Kelmaris. Provides immediate capacity, with annual debt service of roughly VR 55 million at current rates. Risks include weaker fiscal discipline and exposure if take-up exceeds projections.

**Option D: Revenue-neutral redesign of vehicle taxation.** Increase the first-registration tax on high-emission vehicles (top three emission bands) by 12–18 percent and recycle proceeds into rebates. U1 estimates this can fund VR 560 million at plausible elasticities, with an additional VR 180–240 million from closing the diesel company-car concession. Lowest net fiscal cost, but support for buyers of used EVs would need separate funding.

## Assessment

U1's preferred approach is a hybrid: Option D as the primary source, supplemented by a capped Option A appropriation of VR 150 million in FY2026–27 to cover start-up costs and the used-EV stream. Option B is a viable fallback but hypothecation is contrary to U1's established position. Option C is not recommended under current debt targets.

## Next Steps

If the Deputy Minister agrees, U1 will prepare a joint costing annex with the Revenue Forecasting Desk and the Ministry of Transport by 28 March, for inclusion in the FY2026 budget circular.

**Prepared by:** Senior Analyst, Unit U1

**MEMORANDUM — POLICY ANALYSIS**

**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Strategy, Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika
**From:** Unit U1 (Tax Policy)
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives — Revision 2
**Status:** This revision supersedes the memo of 2 February 2025; all cost estimates updated to reflect Q4 revenue outturn from the Port Velmar customs district.

---

**1. Purpose**

U1 has been asked to identify fiscally sustainable financing mechanisms for the proposed National Electric Mobility Incentive Scheme (NEMIS), which combines purchase subsidies and reduced vehicle excise duties. This memo presents updated cost projections and three financing options.

**2. Updated cost estimates**

Revised customs and excise data show that new vehicle registrations in Arunika reached 412,000 units in 2024, of which 9.6% were battery-electric. Projected subsidy outlays under the full NEMIS design are now estimated at ARN 1.48 billion over four years (2026–2029), up ARN 310 million from our February figure, mainly due to higher projected uptake in the Lake Seratia corridor and the industrial belt around Kellmoor. Annual duty relief forgone adds approximately ARN 190 million per year once fully phased in.

**3. Options**

**Option A — Dedicated levy on conventional fuel sales.** A surcharge of ARN 0.11 per litre on petrol and diesel sold nationwide would raise an estimated ARN 620 million annually at current consumption. This is self-reinforcing: as EV uptake grows, the levy base shrinks, creating a natural sunset pressure. Risks: regressive incidence on rural commuters, particularly in the Talvern highlands; potential inflationary effect of 0.3–0.4 percentage points in year one.

**Option B — General budget appropriation.** NEMIS would draw directly from consolidated revenue, with phased caps of ARN 250 million (2026) rising to ARN 480 million (2029). This preserves flexibility and avoids regressive taxes but competes with health and education baselines and is exposed to mid-term austerity revisions, as occurred during the 2022 Veldrin adjustment package.

**Option C — Restructured vehicle ownership tax.** Redirect 40% of annual circulation-tax receipts from internal-combustion vehicles toward NEMIS. We estimate this yields ARN 340–390 million annually, depending on fleet turnover in the Meridian province. This option aligns the incentive with the polluter-pays principle but requires legislative amendment and coordination with the provincial transport registrars.

**4. U1 assessment**

U1's preferred approach is a hybrid: Option A at half the proposed rate (ARN 0.055/litre, yielding ~ARN 310 million) combined with Option C. This covers roughly 85% of projected cost while limiting rural incidence. We recommend that any subsidy be designed with automatic degression, reducing rates 10% annually, to protect against base erosion.

**5. Next steps**

We can provide draft legislative language and a rural-impact correction mechanism (e.g., a rebate for agricultural vehicle registrations) within four weeks, subject to the Deputy Minister's direction.

---
*Unit U1 — Tax Policy Division*

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE, REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U2 (Budget Mandate) — Policy Analysis Memo, Revision 1**

**To:** Deputy Minister, Fiscal Policy Directorate
**From:** Unit U2, Budget Office, Kevana
**Subject:** Financing Options for Electric Vehicle Incentives
**Date:** 14 Meridian 2031

**1. Purpose**
This memo presents U2's assessment of financing options for the proposed National EV Incentive Programme (NEIP), totalling an estimated 1.8 billion arun (ARU) annually through FY2035. Figures reflect U2's internal costings and may differ from those of other units.

**2. Cost Basis**
U2 projects incentive outlays of ARU 1.2b in purchase rebates, ARU 450m in charging-infrastructure grants, and ARU 150m in fleet-conversion credits for the port cities of Selmora and Tel Vasha. Total programme cost: ARU 1.8b/year, equivalent to 0.6% of projected central expenditure.

**3. Option A — General Fund Allocation**
Direct appropriation from the consolidated fund. Pros: simple, no new instruments. Cons: competes with health and education baselines; U2 estimates a 0.3% cut risk to the Municipal Renewal envelope. Sustainability depends on annual appropriations.

**4. Option B — Vehicle Registration Surcharge**
A proposed ARU 400 levy on new internal-combustion vehicles could yield roughly ARU 950m/year, covering about half of programme costs. Pros: partial self-financing, aligned with polluter-pays principles. Cons: U2 models a 6–8% drop in new registrations at dealers in Selmora, with revenue plateauing by FY2034 as the EV share grows — the base erodes by design.

**5. Option C — Green Sovereign Bond**
Issuance of ARU 3.5b in five-year bonds via the Port Kevana treasury desk. Pros: front-loads capital for infrastructure grants; signals credibility to the Velikan Development Partners consortium. Cons: adds ARU 190m/year in debt service; U2 flags verification costs of ARU 25m/year for impact reporting.

**6. Option D — Phased Blended Approach (Recommended)**
U2 recommends a blend: ARU 900m from the general fund, ARU 600m from the registration surcharge (set at ARU 300 initially, rising to ARU 450), and ARU 300m from a scaled bond tranche in FY2032 only. This limits debt service to ARU 65m/year and preserves flexibility if uptake exceeds U2's baseline of 40,000 vehicles annually.

**7. Risks**
(a) Rebate leakage to households already intending to purchase EVs — U2 estimates 20% deadweight; (b) provincial governments in Northmar and Ossery may demand matching grants of up to ARU 120m; (c) surcharge pass-through could lift consumer prices, dampening the rebate effect.

**8. Next Steps**
U2 requests guidance by 28 Meridian to align with the FY2032 budget circular. A joint session with the Revenue Analysis Office and the Infrastructure Coordination Cell in Maru Heights is proposed for the week of 21 Meridian.

**Prepared by:** Unit U2, Budget Office, Kevana
**Status:** Revision 1 — for internal discussion only

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Memorandum U2/2024/EV-05, Revision 2**
**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy
**From:** Unit U2 (Budget)
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives — updated figures
**Date:** 14 October 2024

**Purpose**

This memo revises our earlier analysis (U2/2024/EV-03) in light of updated customs and registration data received from the Port of Selvara collection office and the Office of National Transport Accounts. All figures below supersede those in the previous revision.

**Updated cost estimate**

Demand for the proposed EV purchase incentive has outpaced our original projection. Based on first-half 2024 registration data, we now estimate eligible vehicle purchases at 62,000 units for the first full year of the scheme, against 45,000 assumed previously. At an average incentive of ARN 9,500 per vehicle, the first-year cost rises from ARN 380 million to approximately ARN 590 million, with a five-year cumulative cost of ARN 2.7 billion.

**Option 1: General budget allocation**

Direct allocation from the central budget remains the simplest instrument. The revised cost would require reallocating roughly 1.2% of the discretionary investment envelope in the Velmir District development plan. We assess this as fiscally feasible but note it would delay Phase II of the Karun Bridge project unless offsetting savings are found.

**Option 2: Hypothecated levy on fossil fuels**

A surcharge of ARN 0.4 per litre on motor fuels sold in the western provinces (Tarev, Onsal, and the Northern Basin) would raise an estimated ARN 640 million annually. This would fully cover the scheme and create a self-balancing link between fuel use and EV adoption. Risks include regional price variance and potential pressure on haulage operators in the Onsal corridor, who are already facing margins compressed by last year's freight tariff reform.

**Option 3: Green bond issuance**

Issuing a dedicated bond of ARN 1.5 billion through the National Treasury Agency, anchored to the incentives programme, would spread costs over the medium term. Indications from our contacts at the Doren Merchant Bank suggest demand among regional pension funds is adequate at a coupon of 5.1%. However, debt servicing would add ARN 190 million over the bond's tenor, and the scheme's benefits (mainly to urban households in Selvara and Port Corren) would sit alongside costs borne by all taxpayers.

**Recommendation**

U2 recommends a blended approach: a general allocation of ARN 300 million in year one, complemented by a fossil fuel levy of ARN 0.25 per litre limited to the three western provinces, and a smaller bond of ARN 500 million. This spreads the burden without over-hypothecation and preserves the Karun Bridge schedule.

**Next steps**

We request the Deputy Minister's guidance before 28 October to allow inclusion in the supplementary budget bill. Unit U2 will prepare drafting instructions for the levy legislation once the financing mix is confirmed.

*Prepared by Unit U2 (Budget). Internal working document — not for distribution.*

# MEMORANDUM

**To:** Honourable Minister of Finance, Republic of Arunika
**From:** Unit U3 (Treasury Mandate)
**Subject:** Financing Options for Electric Vehicle Incentives
**Revision:** 1
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Classification:** Internal – Draft for Discussion

---

## 1. Purpose

This memo, prepared solely from Unit U3's treasury perspective, sets out financing options for the proposed National EV Purchase Incentive Programme (NEVIP), estimated by this unit at **Arunika Shillings (AS) 1.85 billion** over three fiscal years (FY26–FY28). All figures below are U3 internal estimates and have not yet been cleared by the Fiscal Policy Office or the Department of Budget Control.

## 2. Fiscal Context

U3 projects a consolidated deficit of AS 12.4 billion for FY26, with net domestic borrowing of AS 7.9 billion. The Treasury Cash Account at the Port Kessani Revenue House currently holds a buffer of AS 2.1 billion. Debt service already absorbs 18.3% of revenue, and U3 assesses limited room for new borrowing without pressure on the yield curve.

## 3. Options Considered

**Option A – Direct budget allocation.** Fund NEVIP from annual appropriations (AS 620 million per year). U3 notes this competes with the Meridian Road Upgrade and the Highland Water Scheme. Risk: mid-year cuts, as occurred in FY24 when the Solar Rooftop Rebate was reduced by 22%.

**Option B – Earmarked levy.** Introduce a AS 0.15/litre surcharge on petroleum imports channelled through the Energy Transition Fund administered by the Keluwara Fund Secretariat. U3 estimates yield of AS 780 million annually, fully covering the programme. However, U3 cautions that earmarking constrains treasury flexibility and the levy is regressive.

**Option C – Green bond issuance.** Issue a AS 1.2 billion sovereign green bond maturing 2031. U3's preliminary pricing suggests a coupon of 8.4%, roughly 90 basis points above conventional yields, implying an incremental cost of AS 11 million per year. Verification costs through an external standards body are estimated at AS 6 million annually.

**Option D – Hybrid (recommended by U3).** Combine a phased budget allocation of AS 900 million over three years with a AS 950 million green bond. This smooths annual appropriations and reduces single-source risk.

## 4. U3 Assessment

U3 favours Option D. It limits incremental borrowing, avoids a regressive levy, and preserves the FY26 cash buffer. The unit's cash-flow model shows peak outlays in FY27 (AS 710 million) coinciding with projected bond proceeds.

## 5. Risks

- Bond market appetite for Arunikan paper is untested; U3 assumes placement via the Norevai Primary Dealers Group.
- Incentive uptake may exceed forecasts by up to 30%, requiring a contingency line of AS 140 million.
- Coordination with the Ministry of Transport's registry system remains unresolved.

## 6. Next Steps

U3 seeks the Minister's steer by 31 March 2025 to meet the FY26 budget calendar, and proposes a joint session with the Budget Control Department and the Keluwara Fund Secretariat in early April.

---

*Prepared by Unit U3. Figures are U3 estimates, subject to revision.*

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Memo U3-25/114, Revision 2**
**From:** Unit U3 (Treasury)
**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives — updated figures

**1. Purpose**
This revision supersedes Memo U3-25/114 of 21 January 2025. It restates the financing options for the national EV incentive programme using updated revenue and uptake projections from the Office of Tax Forecasting in New Kelvar and the Regional Treasury Bureau at Port Sendra. Conclusions are unchanged; figures are not.

**2. Cost of the programme**
Our revised baseline puts the cost of purchase rebates and charging-infrastructure grants at AR 410 million per year for 2025–2029, up from AR 355 million in the previous draft. The increase reflects faster-than-expected uptake in the Meridian Valley pilot region, where rebate applications are running 22% above forecast. Total five-year cost is now AR 2,050 million.

**3. Option A — General budget allocation**
Drawing from general revenue is simple and avoids earmarking rigidities. However, U3 estimates the 2025 fiscal deficit at AR 1,240 million, and a further AR 410 million outlay would push debt service toward 17% of revenue by 2028. We assess this option as feasible but fiscal-risk-prone.

**4. Option B — Dedicated levy on fuel imports**
A surcharge of AR 0.40 per litre on imported fuel, administered through the Customs Bureau at Port Sendra, would raise approximately AR 460 million per year at projected import volumes. This more than covers the programme and is plausibly self-limiting as EV adoption reduces fuel imports. Risk: revenue erosion in later years, and a regressive incidence on rural motorists in the Northern Highlands. We estimate revenue falling below AR 300 million by 2032 under the high-uptake scenario.

**5. Option C — Green bond issuance**
Issuing a five-year green bond of AR 1,800 million via the National Debt Office would match the programme's duration. Current market soundings suggest a coupon of 6.1%, roughly 45 basis points above conventional issues. This front-loads funding and locks in costs, but adds AR 550 million in cumulative interest over the term.

**6. U3 view**
We recommend a hybrid: Option B for roughly two-thirds of annual cost, with the remainder from the general budget, kept flexible to hedge against fuel-levy revenue erosion. We advise against full bond financing at current spreads. If the fuel levy proves politically unworkable, Option A remains the fallback, ideally paired with an annual review clause so U3 can reprice the programme each budget cycle.

**7. Next steps**
Feedback from the Office of Tax Forecasting and the Debt Office is requested by 28 March 2025 so a final recommendation can accompany the spring budget annex.

Prepared by Unit U3 (Treasury).

# POLICY ANALYSIS MEMO

**Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika**
**Unit U3 (Treasury Mandate)**
**Revision 3 — supersedes Revisions 1 and 2; figures updated**
**Date: 14 March 2025**
**Subject: Financing options for electric vehicle incentives**

**1. Purpose**

This memo sets out Unit U3's assessment of financing options for the proposed National EV Incentive Programme (NEVIP), covering purchase subsidies, charging infrastructure grants, and fleet conversion support. All figures are Unit U3's own estimates and may differ from those of other units.

**2. Updated cost projections**

Revised take-up assumptions from the Vehicle Registry Office in Kelmora indicate higher demand than previously modelled. U3 now projects incentive outlays of AR 1.9 billion over five years (Revision 2 estimate: AR 1.4 billion). Annual profile: AR 210 million (Year 1), AR 390 million (Year 2), AR 450 million (Year 3), peaking at AR 480 million (Year 4), before declining to AR 370 million (Year 5). Charging infrastructure grants add an estimated AR 320 million over the period, concentrated in the Thesselport and Ardenvale corridors.

**3. Financing options assessed**

*Option A — General budget allocation.* Drawn from the Consolidated Fund. Simple and transparent, but exposes the annual budget cycle to volatility; Year 4 peak spending would require AR 480 million in a single fiscal year, roughly 0.6% of projected central expenditure.

*Option B — Dedicated green levy.* A surcharge of AR 0.12 per litre on transport fuels, administered through the Revenue Collection Directorate in Sarnvale. U3 estimates annual yield of AR 340–390 million, broadly matching the spending profile. Risk: yields decline as EV adoption grows, creating a fiscal cliff in Years 6–8.

*Option C — Green bond issuance.* The Debt Management Office in Port Halloran estimates that a AR 1.5 billion, seven-year green bond could be placed at a spread of 45–60 basis points above conventional paper. Proceeds would smooth front-loaded costs. Compliance and certification costs estimated at AR 6 million annually.

*Option D — Blended structure (recommended).* Combine a phased levy (Option B) covering roughly 60% of costs with a smaller bond (Option C) of AR 700 million for infrastructure grants, and draw down AR 150 million from the Rainy Day Contingency Account in Year 1 to bridge the ramp-up.

**4. U3 assessment**

Option D best matches revenues to the spending curve while limiting borrowing. U3 estimates net fiscal cost of AR 95 million over five years, versus AR 1.9 billion under Option A. Key risks: legislative delay on the levy (mitigated by contingency drawdown) and reputational risk if bond proceeds are redirected (mitigated by ring-fenced reporting to the Audit Chamber of Brelyn).

**5. Recommendation**

U3 recommends adoption of Option D, with a decision paper to the Minister by 30 April 2025 to allow bond preparation ahead of the autumn issuance window.

**REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA — MINISTRY OF FINANCE**
**Unit U4 (Public Debt Management)**

**POLICY ANALYSIS MEMO — REVISION 1**
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**To:** Office of the Vice-Minister for Fiscal Policy
**From:** Unit U4, Public Debt Management
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives

---

**1. Purpose**

This memo examines funding sources for the proposed National Electric Mobility Scheme (NEMS), which would offer purchase subsidies of up to 8,500 aurans per vehicle. Unit U4 assesses the options from a debt-management perspective only; policy design rests with U2 (Transport Economics).

**2. Fiscal context**

The Department of Budgetary Affairs estimates NEMS costs at 310 million aurans in FY2026, rising to 520 million by FY2029 as uptake accelerates. Arunika's debt-to-GDP ratio stands at 61.4%, and the medium-term fiscal framework commits the Treasury to keeping new net borrowing below 2.8% of GDP. NEMS, if funded entirely through issuance, would add roughly 0.4 percentage points to the borrowing requirement in the peak year.

**3. Options assessed**

**Option A — Direct issuance.** Financing via the regular bond programme (the Meridian benchmark series). Pros: simple, transparent, preserves unified funding. Cons: adds duration to a market already absorbing 2.1 billion aurans of net issuance; the Debt Office in Port Kalindre flags possible yield pressure of 15–25 basis points at the long end.

**Option B — Ring-fenced green bond.** A dedicated "Arunika Clean Mobility Bond" of 450 million aurans, eligible under the Treasury's draft green framework. Pros: broadens the investor base; the Capital Markets Liaison Office reports strong interest from two regional pension funds in Verensa. Cons: issuance costs an estimated 8–12 basis points higher; ring-fencing constrains treasury flexibility and creates re-funding risk at maturity.

**Option C — Hypothecated levy.** A 1.9% surcharge on vehicle registration fees, hypothecated to NEMS. Pros: no new debt; aligns cost with users. Cons: revenue (est. 240–280 million aurans annually) is volatile and lags uptake; the Revenue Analysis Division cautions that hypothecation reduces budget flexibility and may require a floor grant if uptake outpaces collections.

**Option D — Blended structure.** Roughly 60% levy, 40% issuance via the green bond. Pros: smooths market impact and diversifies sources; consistent with the Debt Office's medium-term funding diversification target. Cons: administrative complexity; requires inter-unit coordination on cash-flow timing.

**4. Unit U4 view**

U4 prefers **Option D**, with the green bond share capped at 500 million aurans to preserve flexibility. Should the levy prove unreliable in its first two years, the fallback is **Option A**, accepting modest yield pressure. U4 does not recommend full hypothecation (Option C) given revenue volatility, nor a large standalone green bond (Option B) until the green framework is formally accredited.

**5. Next steps**

U4 requests guidance by 28 March 2025 to align the funding plan with the FY2026 pre-budget calendar. U4 will prepare a cash-flow annex and an investor communication note thereafter.

**Prepared by:** Unit U4, Public Debt Management
**Status:** Revision 1 — for internal discussion; figures are U4 estimates and subject to change.

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U4 (Public Debt and Debt Management)**

**MEMORANDUM — REVISION 2**
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives — updated figures
**Classification:** Internal — For Official Use

**1. Purpose**

This memo updates Revision 1 (dated 2 February 2025) in light of the revised revenue outturn published by the Budget Directorate in late February and the updated borrowing calendar agreed with the Central Bank of Arunika. Figures below supersede those in Revision 1; conclusions are broadly unchanged.

**2. Context**

The Ministry of Transport has proposed a purchase-subsidy scheme for electric vehicles totalling AR 480 million per year over five years (AR 2.4 billion total), up from AR 420 million per year in the earlier proposal. Unit U4's mandate is public debt management; we assess the options from the standpoint of debt sustainability and market impact only. Policy merit is outside our remit.

**3. Financing options**

**Option A — Annual budget allocation.** Fund the subsidy from annual appropriations. Given the revised fiscal position (deficit now projected at 4.6% of GDP versus 4.2% assumed in Revision 1), full absorption would raise the 2025 borrowing requirement to approximately AR 1.9 billion. This is feasible but would crowd out allocations to the Northhaven Road Rehabilitation Programme unless offset.

**Option B — Dedicated bond issuance.** Issue a five-year "Green Transition Bond" for AR 2.4 billion. Preliminary soundings by the Debt Management Office suggest demand of roughly AR 3.1 billion from the Arunika Pension Fund and two regional banks in Velmour and Kestrel Bay, at an estimated yield of 7.8%, about 40 basis points above comparable conventional paper. Interest costs over the term would total approximately AR 520 million. This preserves budget room but adds a marked benchmark issuance to the calendar.

**Option C — Phased drawdown from the Stabilisation and Reserve Fund.** A phased withdrawal of AR 480 million per year would reduce the Fund to AR 3.9 billion by 2030, still above the statutory floor of AR 3.0 billion. This avoids new debt but weakens the buffer ahead of the 2027 external refinancing peak (AR 2.2 billion falling due).

**4. Assessment**

Option A is the simplest but strains the deficit. Option C is attractive until 2027, but tapering withdrawals from 2026 would be prudent. Option B carries the highest fiscal cost but offers a useful yield benchmark and, if labelled green, may attract concessional refinancing later in the decade. A hybrid — Fund drawdown for the first two years, bond issuance in year three — appears to U4 to balance cost and risk best.

**5. Recommendation**

That the Minister instruct the Budget Directorate and the Debt Management Office to prepare a hybrid financing plan along the lines of Section 4, for decision before the April budget round.

**Unit U4 — Public Debt and Debt Management**

Cleared by: Director, U4

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE, REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U4 — Public Debt Management**

**MEMORANDUM — Revision 3 (supersedes Rev. 2, March 2025)**

**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy
**From:** Unit U4 (Public Debt)
**Date:** 12 May 2025
**Subject:** Financing options for electric vehicle incentives — updated figures

**Purpose**

This memo updates the financing analysis in Revision 2 following the National Statistics Office of Velmora's revised EV adoption forecast. The revised estimate projects 180,000 EV registrations by 2028, up from 140,000, raising the gross cost of the proposed purchase-subsidy programme from ARN 2.1 billion to ARN 2.9 billion over the period. All figures below are U4's own estimates.

**Cost profile**

The revised programme implies annual outlays of ARN 0.5 billion (2025), ARN 0.8 billion (2026), ARN 0.9 billion (2027), and ARN 0.7 billion (2028), assuming a subsidy taper from ARN 8,000 to ARN 4,000 per vehicle. Administered by the Vehicle Incentive Office in Kaldren, roughly 15% of outlays are expected to be disbursed in the following fiscal year, smoothing cash requirements.

**Option A — Budget appropriation**

Direct annual appropriations from the central budget preserve clarity and avoid debt issuance. However, the fiscal outlook (U4 working paper 25/07) shows limited headroom: the primary surplus of 1.2% of GDP leaves little room for new discretionary spending without breaching the deficit corridor of 2.8%. A dedicated allocation would likely require cuts elsewhere.

**Option B — Dedicated green bond issuance**

U4 assesses that an "Arunika Sustainable Mobility Bond" of ARN 2.0 billion, issued in tranches over 2025–2026, could be placed with investors in the Solvenn capital market at an estimated coupon of 5.4%, roughly 60 basis points above conventional 7-year yields. The premium reflects limited investor appetite demonstrated at the Port Hadrell green financing roundtable last year. Debt servicing would total approximately ARN 0.55 billion through 2032, extending obligations beyond the subsidy period.

**Option C — Phased hybrid**

A blended approach: ARN 1.2 billion in appropriations for the 2025–2026 ramp-up, plus a ARN 1.7 billion bond tranche in 2027 when adoption peaks. This matches debt-financing to the heaviest outlay years while limiting the green premium to one issuance. U4 estimates blended cost at ARN 0.45 billion in servicing and forgone budget room combined.

**Assessment**

U4's mandate emphasises debt sustainability. Option C best balances near-term fiscal constraints against the risk of locking in elevated coupons for the full programme. Option B remains viable if the Treasury Office in Renvale can negotiate the premium below 40 basis points. Option A is fiscally clean but unlikely to be sustainable at revised volumes.

**Recommendation**

U4 recommends Option C, with delegation to the Deputy Minister to authorise pre-mandate soundings with the Solvenn primary dealers by June 2025. Unit U4 will circulate updated costing if adoption forecasts change again.

**U4 — Public Debt Management**
Drafted: Senior Analyst, Debt Strategy Desk, Unit U4

# Policy Analysis Memo — Revision 1

**Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika**
**Unit U1 (Tax Policy)**
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Subject:** Redesigning rural electrification financing
**Prepared by:** U1 Lead Analyst, Senior Desk for Energy Taxation
**For:** Office of the Deputy Minister for Fiscal Planning

## Purpose

This memo presents U1's assessment of the current rural electrification financing framework and proposes a redesigned structure. All figures reflect U1's tax-policy perspective and internal estimates as of Q1 2025.

## Background

The current Rural Power Access Scheme, administered by the Directorate of Regional Energy (DRE), is funded primarily through the National Electrification Levy (NEL), a 3.2% surcharge on commercial electricity bills. U1 estimates NEL revenue at AR 84 billion annually, against program outlays of AR 112 billion, producing a structural gap of roughly AR 28 billion per year. Coverage in the provinces of Meraval, Tondari, and South Kelanti remains below 55%.

## Problems Identified

1. **Regressive incidence.** The NEL falls on commercial electricity consumption, which U1 modeling suggests is passed through to consumers, including low-income urban households with no connection to the program's benefits.
2. **Revenue instability.** NEL receipts have fluctuated between AR 71 and 92 billion over the past four fiscal years, complicating DRE planning.
3. **Weak cost recovery.** Connection-fee rebates administered by the Field Services Office (Fennwick Branch) recover only 9% of installation costs, per U1 calculations.
4. **Leakage.** U1 audit sampling indicates AR 3.4 billion in misclassified commercial exemptions in FY 2024.

## Proposed Redesign

U1 recommends a three-part structure:

- **Broadened base.** Replace the NEL with a Tiered Energy Access Levy (TEAL) of 1.8% on all electricity consumption above 200 kWh/month, residential and commercial. U1 projects stable revenue of AR 96–101 billion, with incidence shifting toward higher-consumption households.
- **Rural connection tax credit.** Introduce a refundable credit of AR 450,000 per new rural connection claimed by licensed distributors, conditional on verified installation in designated districts (initially Meraval and Tondari). Estimated cost: AR 21 billion/year, plausibly lifting annual connections from 38,000 to 55,000.
- **Local surtax sharing.** Allow provincial treasuries in South Kelanti to retain 15% of TEAL collected locally, funding last-mile maintenance. Expected yield: AR 6 billion/year.

## Fiscal Impact

Net U1-estimated effect: the gap narrows from AR 28 billion to approximately AR 9 billion by FY 2027, with the remainder addressed by DRE expenditure rationalization (outside U1's mandate).

## Risks and Caveats

- Distributors in the Harlan Valley pilot zone may resist credit verification burdens.
- TEAL's residential inclusion carries political sensitivity; U1 recommends paired messaging with the connection credit.
- Revenue projections assume no consumption contraction above the 200 kWh threshold; elasticity assumptions are conservative but untested.

## Next Steps

U1 will circulate draft legislation language to DRE and the Office of Budget Expenditure by 30 April 2025 and requests the Deputy Minister's decision on the credit's refundability before then.

— Unit U1, Tax Policy

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Policy Analysis Memo — Unit U1 (Tax Policy)**

**Subject:** Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing
**Revision:** 2 (supersedes Revision 1 of March; figures updated per new data from the Regional Revenue Offices of Kelawi and Doruma)
**Date:** 12 May
**Distribution:** Deputy Minister's Office; Directorate of Budget; Rural Energy Taskforce

**Purpose**
This memo updates U1's earlier assessment of financing options for the National Rural Electrification Programme (NREP), reflecting revised revenue projections and new collections data.

**Revised Fiscal Picture**
Revision 1 estimated an annual financing gap of 310 million aruns. Updated figures from the Kelawi and Doruma Regional Revenue Offices raise the projected gap to 365 million aruns for FY-2027, mainly because corporate tax receipts from the mining sector in the Doruma belt are now expected to fall 9% below prior estimates. Diesel fuel excise receipts, previously assumed at 48 million aruns, are revised to 41 million aruns as rural distributors shift to solar-hybrid mini-grids.

**Assessment of Current Instruments**
The existing mechanism—a 2.5% levy on commercial electricity tariffs—will yield an estimated 95 million aruns in FY-2027, up from 88 million in Revision 1 due to improved compliance in urban distribution companies. However, the levy is regressive: households in the Vantara and Selu districts bear a disproportionate share relative to grid coverage received. U1 does not recommend raising the levy above 3%; modelling suggests marginal collection costs rise sharply beyond that threshold, and pass-through to small enterprises would offset employment gains targeted by the NREP.

**Recommended Redesign**
U1 proposes a three-part package, on which this unit's estimates are as follows:

1. **Rural connection tax credit.** A credit of 1,800 aruns per new household connection, claimable against corporate income tax by licensed distributors, capped at 130 million aruns annually. Cost is offset by an estimated 55 million aruns in secondary VAT receipts from newly connected commercial users.

2. **Reallocation of the fuel excise base.** Redirect 30 million aruns of the revised 41 million in diesel excise receipts to a Rural Access Fund, administered jointly with the Doruma Development Authority.

3. **Targeted import duty relief.** Exempt solar panels and storage units below 5 kW from the current 12% duty, at a static cost of 74 million aruns. U1 estimates dynamic cost at 58 million aruns once installer-sector formalisation is factored in.

**Risks and Caveats**
Tax-credit uptake may concentrate in the better-served Kelawi corridor; U1 recommends a floor requiring 40% of claimed connections in underserved districts. Figures are U1's own and do not reflect the Directorate of Budget's expenditure-side costing; coordination with that directorate is required before Cabinet submission.

**Recommendation**
U1 recommends the three-part package above, with a review scheduled after two fiscal years, as providing a more equitable and durable financing base than tariff levy expansion.

Prepared by: Unit U1, Tax Policy Division

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U1 (Tax Policy) — Policy Analysis Memo, Revision 3**
**Subject: Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing**
**Date: 14 March 2025** | **Supersedes Revisions 1 and 2 (of 2 January and 11 February 2025)**

**Purpose**
This memo updates U1's analysis of rural electrification financing in light of the new Kavara District connection data released by the National Statistics Office of Arunika (NSOA) in February. All figures are U1's own estimates and do not represent a Ministry-wide position.

**Background**
Current financing relies on a flat 4 aruni-per-litre levy on diesel transported to rural grid stations, plus annual budget transfers from the General Reserve Fund. Revision 2 estimated levy receipts at 220 million arunis for FY2025. Updated NSOA data on diesel volumes in Kavara, Selumbu, and the Upper Dranis provinces shows a larger formalised distribution base than previously assumed.

**Updated Findings**
1. Levy receipts are now projected at 268 million arunis for FY2025, 22% above the Revision 2 estimate, chiefly because informal diesel flows into the Dranis corridor have been reclassified. Collections by the Regional Revenue Office in Kavara alone rose to 41 million arunis.
2. However, revenue remains volatile: diesel consumption in connected villages falls by an estimated 6–9% once households switch to grid electricity, eroding the levy base over time. U1 projects receipts declining to roughly 205 million arunis by FY2029 if the levy is unchanged.
3. The proposed connection fee of 350 arunis per household, modelled in Revision 2, now looks too high: survey data from Selumbu suggest willingness to pay is closer to 240 arunis, and collection costs via Local Revenue Desks would absorb 12% of gross receipts.

**Options Considered**
*Option A — Retain the diesel levy.* Simple, but a shrinking base and regressive incidence on households not yet connected.
*Option B — Replace the levy with a 1.5% surcharge on commercial electricity tariffs nationwide.* Broader base; U1 estimates 310–340 million arunis annually, though it raises industrial tariffs in cities such as Port Meruna, which the Ministry of Trade is likely to resist.
*Option C — Hybrid.* Reduce the diesel levy to 2.5 arunis per litre and add a 0.8% tariff surcharge, yielding an estimated 280 million arunis with lower volatility and moderate incidence.

**Recommendation**
U1 recommends Option C, with two safeguards: (i) the surcharge should sunset after five years pending review by the Joint Fiscal Review Committee; and (ii) connection fees should be cut to 240 arunis and administered through mobile payment channels to reduce collection costs to an estimated 5%.

**Caveats**
Projections assume NSOA's diesel formalisation figures are accurate; a joint verification exercise with the Kavara Revenue Office is advisable before FY2026 budgeting. This memo does not assess distributional effects outside U1's mandate.

**Next Steps**
Consultations with the Directorate of Energy Planning and the General Reserve Fund Office in April; revised revenue model to follow as Revision 4.

*Prepared by Unit U1, Tax Policy*

# POLICY ANALYSIS MEMO — REVISION 1

**Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika**
**Unit U2 (Budget Mandate)**
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Subject:** Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing
**Distribution:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy; Director of Unit U2
**File:** U2-2025-018

---

**Purpose**

This memo presents Unit U2's assessment of the current rural electrification financing framework and proposes a revised structure, from a budget-management perspective. All figures reflect U2's internal estimates and may differ from those held by other units.

**Current Situation**

The National Rural Grid Programme (NRGP), administered through the Directorate of Energy Access in Kelumar, is financed through annual budget appropriations of approximately ARN 4.2 billion, supplemented by concessional loans channelled via the Provincial Development Bank of Soravi. U2 estimates that only 63% of appropriated funds are disbursed within the fiscal year, with an average carryover of ARN 1.4 billion. Cost per connection has risen from ARN 41,000 in 2021 to ARN 58,000 in 2024, driven largely by terrain costs in the highland districts of Tavren and Oskemi.

**Key Problems Identified**

1. **Rigid annual appropriation cycle.** Grid extensions are multi-year projects, yet funding is released in single-year tranches, causing contractor suspension in lowland provinces such as Delva Maru.
2. **Weak cost recovery.** Tariff revenues collected by the rural cooperatives recover only 28% of operating costs, creating a recurring call on the budget of roughly ARN 700 million per year.
3. **Concentration risk.** 71% of outstanding programme debt is concentrated in the Soravi lending window, limiting fiscal flexibility.

**Proposed Redesign**

U2 recommends a three-pillar structure:

- **Pillar 1 — Multi-year rolling envelope.** Convert NRGP appropriations into a three-year envelope of ARN 13.8 billion, with annual releases conditional on verified disbursement ratios of at least 75%.
- **Pillar 2 — Ring-fenced maintenance fund.** Establish a Rural Grid Maintenance Fund, capitalised at ARN 900 million, financed by a dedicated levy of ARN 30 per megawatt-hour on urban distribution revenues, to replace the ARN 700 million annual budget subsidy over three years.
- **Pillar 3 — Diversified borrowing.** Cap Soravi window exposure at 50% of programme debt and pre-authorise up to ARN 2 billion in municipal bond issuance by the Kelumar and Port Hemris utilities against connection revenues.

**Fiscal Implications**

U2 projects net budget savings of ARN 450 million by Year 3, assuming levy collection efficiency of 85%. Transition costs of ARN 220 million in Year 1 are expected, principally for cooperative tariff reform support in the Nekesa valley region.

**Risks**

Levy pass-through to urban consumers may face political resistance; U2 assesses this as manageable if phased in two steps of ARN 15 per megawatt-hour. Bond issuance depends on audited revenue streams not yet verified.

**Recommendation**

U2 recommends that the Deputy Minister endorse the three-pillar redesign for inclusion in the 2026 budget circular, subject to a joint review with the energy directorate by June 2025.

---
*Prepared by Unit U2. Figures are unit estimates for internal discussion.*

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U2 (Budget Policy) — Policy Analysis Memo, Revision 2**
**Date: 14 May 2025**
**Subject: Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing**

**1. Purpose**

This memo updates the findings of Revision 1 (dated 3 April 2025) to reflect new cost and revenue figures supplied by the Provincial Treasury Offices of Kelara and Vondama. It recommends a revised financing structure for the national rural electrification programme. All figures are Unit U2's own estimates and do not represent Ministry-wide positions.

**2. Revised Findings**

The first revision estimated a funding gap of 380 million surins for fiscal years 2026–2028. Updated provincial data from the Kelara District Energy Office and the Vondama Grid Extension Bureau raise that gap to 455 million surins. The increase is driven mainly by higher connection costs in dispersed settlements: connection cost per household in remote provinces is now estimated at 9,800 surins, against 6,200 surins in Revision 1.

On the revenue side, updated household payment data from the Solma Electricity Cooperative show collection rates of 78 percent in grid-connected villages, up from 71 percent assumed earlier, but only 44 percent in off-grid villages served by mini-grids. This confirms that tariff-based cost recovery alone cannot sustain the programme.

**3. Problems with the Current Structure**

The current model relies on a single Central Electrification Grant Line covering 85 percent of capital costs, with provincial governments covering the remainder. Three problems persist:

- Provincial co-financing has lagged; only 62 percent of pledged provincial contributions were disbursed in FY2025.
- The grant line crowds out maintenance, which Unit U2 estimates is underfunded by 55 million surins annually.
- Mini-grid operators in areas such as the Dresta Valley receive no operational subsidy, leading to service shutdowns in eleven villages this year.

**4. Revised Recommendation**

Unit U2 recommends a three-pillar redesign, with updated figures:

- **Capital pillar:** Reduce the central grant to 65 percent of capital costs but add a Remote Access Top-Up of 1,900 surins per connection for households beyond 5 kilometres of existing lines, costing an estimated 92 million surins through 2028.
- **Operations pillar:** Create a Mini-Grid Viability Fund of 28 million surins per year, financed by reallocating 15 million surins from the urban grid subsidy and raising 13 million surins through a modest connection levy in metered urban districts.
- **Accountability pillar:** Require provincial treasuries to submit annual co-financing certificates; disbursing central grants in two tranches, the second conditional on verified provincial deposits, would limit leakage to an estimated 4 percent, down from 11 percent.

**5. Fiscal Implications**

The redesign is broadly neutral for the central budget: additional top-up and fund costs of roughly 120 million surins over three years are offset by reduced central grants and lower leakage. Net fiscal impact is estimated at a 9 million surins saving.

**6. Next Steps**

If endorsed, Unit U2 will draft budget-line instructions before the FY2026 budget submission in August, in coordination with the Provincial Treasury Offices.

**Prepared by:** Unit U2, Budget Policy Division

MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA
Unit U3 (Treasury and Public Finance)
Policy Analysis Memo — Revision 1
Date: 14 March 2025
To: Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy
From: Unit U3, Office of Treasury Planning
Subject: Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing

1. Purpose
This memo presents U3's view on restructuring the financing framework for the National Rural Electrification Programme (NREP), ahead of the FY2026 budget cycle. Figures herein reflect U3 estimates only and have not been reconciled with Unit U7 (Energy Sector Analysis).

2. Problem
The NREP is currently financed through annual budget transfers to the Rural Power Agency (RPA), supplemented by the Kethara Energy Levy (0.8% on commercial electricity bills). U3 projects a funding gap of Arunikan goldmarks (AGM) 214 million in FY2026, rising to AGM 380 million by FY2028. Annual appropriations create stop-start implementation: connection rates in the Maruvani and Delowa provinces fell 22% last year after a mid-year budget revision. Treasury cash-flow records also show the RPA holds an average idle balance of AGM 61 million, indicating weak cash management rather than genuine absorption capacity.

3. Current Financing Mix (U3 estimates, FY2025)
- Annual budget appropriations: AGM 410m (64%)
- Kethara Energy Levy: AGM 145m (23%)
- Provincial co-contributions: AGM 55m (9%)
- Donor grants (Westvale Facility): AGM 28m (4%)

4. U3 Assessment
The current mix over-relies on the discretionary annual budget and under-uses stable revenue instruments. The levy is underexploited: U3 modelling suggests a rise from 0.8% to 1.2% would yield an additional AGM 96m annually with negligible inflationary effect. However, earmarking of levy proceeds weakens treasury control and fragments the budget. U3 therefore favours consolidation of revenue flows into a multi-year envelope, not expanded earmarking.

5. Proposal (U3 position)
a. Replace annual appropriations with a three-year rolling NREP envelope of AGM 1.15 billion, approved once by Parliament, released through a certified quarterly schedule tied to verified connection milestones.
b. Raise the Kethara Energy Levy to 1.2%, with proceeds pooled centrally and distributed via the envelope, not directly to the RPA.
c. Introduce a debt facility through the National Development Fund (NdF) of up to AGM 150m at 3.1% concessional rate, repayable over 12 years from the envelope. U3 estimates debt service at AGM 14m annually, well within envelope capacity.
d. Require the RPA to consolidate idle balances into the Single Treasury Account, releasing an estimated AGM 55m for programming.

6. Fiscal Impact (U3 estimates)
Net budget savings of AGM 40m in FY2026, rising to AGM 90m by FY2028, driven mainly by avoided idle balances and reduced borrowing at commercial rates. Contingent liability exposure from the NdF facility is assessed at AGM 12m (expected-loss basis).

7. Risks
- Political resistance to a further levy increase; mitigation: phased increase (0.2% per year).
- Verification capacity of connection milestones remains weak; U3 recommends an audit protocol with the Office of the Auditor-General of Arunika by Q2 FY2026.

8. Recommendation
U3 requests the Deputy Minister's endorsement of the three-year envelope proposal for inclusion in the FY2026 budget framework, and a joint session with U7 to reconcile energy-sector assumptions before final submission.

Prepared by: Unit U3, Office of Treasury Planning

**MEMORANDUM — REVISION 2**

**To:** Office of the Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy, Ministry of Finance, Republic of Arunika
**From:** Unit U3 (Treasury Mandate)
**Date:** 14 Frimaire, Year 12
**Subject:** Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing — Updated Treasury Findings

---

**Purpose**

This memo supersedes Revision 1 (dated 2 Frimaire) of Unit U3's analysis of the Rural Electrification Financing Framework (REFF). Revisions reflect audited disbursement data from the Velloran Provincial Treasury and revised load-growth projections supplied by the Kessari District Field Office. All figures are U3's own estimates and should not be read as whole-of-ministry positions.

**Updated Fiscal Position**

Audited figures raise the projected four-year financing gap for the REFF from 41.7 to 48.3 million runats. The change stems mainly from slower-than-assumed household connection rates in the Toruva Basin, which have extended subsidy disbursements per connection from 9,200 to 11,400 runats. The Contingency Reserve at the Velloran Treasury Office now stands at 12.1 million runats — sufficient for 2.1 years at current burn rates, down from 3.4 years estimated in Revision 1.

**Assessment of the Current Design**

The existing blended structure (40% central grant, 35% concessional debt through the Provincial Lending Window, 25% municipal match) continues to underperform. U3's updated modelling indicates:

- The municipal match requirement excludes 14 of Arunika's 31 rural municipalities, up from 11 in Revision 1, owing to revised revenue-base calculations for the Semru and Odivar regions.
- Debt servicing on the concessional tranche consumes 6.8% of municipal operating budgets in recipient districts, versus 4.9% assumed previously.
- Cost per sustained connection (retained after 24 months) has risen to 15,900 runats against a planning benchmark of 12,500.

**Revised Recommendations**

U3 maintains the direction of Revision 1 but adjusts parameters:

1. Replace the flat 40% central grant with a tiered grant (55% for municipalities below the 40th income percentile, 35% otherwise). Estimated incremental cost: 3.9 million runats annually, offset by the reduced municipal match (lowered from 25% to 15%).
2. Convert the concessional debt window into a revolving fund seeded with 18 million runats from the Contingency Reserve, recycled over an 11-year horizon. U3 projects net fiscal savings of 7.2 million runats over the medium term.
3. Defer the proposed rural tariff adjustment — the updated connection elasticity estimate (-1.4 versus -0.9) implies greater uptake risk than previously modelled.

**Fiscal Risk and Sequencing**

The largest risk remains disbursement leakage in the Toruva and Kessari corridors, estimated at 4.2% of flows, down from 5.6% following the new audit protocols. U3 recommends piloting the tiered grant in the Semru region in the next fiscal year before national rollout.

U3 requests a decision from the Deputy Minister by the end of the quarter to align with the provincial budget calendar.

— Unit U3, Treasury Mandate

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U4 (Public Debt Management) — Policy Analysis Memo**

**To:** Deputy Minister for Fiscal Policy
**From:** Unit U4 — Public Debt and Financing Structures
**Date:** 14 March 2025
**Re:** Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing
**Status:** Revision 1 (supersedes draft of 21 February 2025)

**Purpose**

This memo presents Unit U4's assessment of options for financing the National Rural Electrification Program (NREP) in light of rising debt-service pressure. Figures reflect our unit's own estimates and should be reconciled with the Budget Directorate before Cabinet submission.

**Problem**

The NREP is financed through annual budget transfers plus sovereign guarantees for the Rural Power Agency (RPA). Our projections show guaranteed RPA debt reaching Arunika rupees (AR) 340 billion by 2028, or 4.1% of GDP, with contingency liabilities concentrated in three provinces (Meru Basin, Halvet Highlands, Solano Delta). Current design places repayment risk fully on the sovereign, while tariff collection rates in target districts average only 62%.

**Options Considered**

*Option A — Status quo.* Budget allocations of AR 85 billion annually plus unlimited RPA guarantees. Highest sovereign exposure; not recommended.

*Option B — Ring-fenced electrification fund.* A dedicated Rural Energy Finance Facility (REFF) would issue bonds against a blended revenue base: connection fees, a AR 2 per kWh rural tariff surcharge, and concessional inflows. We estimate this could mobilize AR 210 billion over five years while reducing contingent liabilities by roughly 35%.

*Option C — Partial credit enhancement.* Guarantee only 50–60% of RPA borrowing from the Meridian Regional Development Bank (a fictional regional lender) and require co-lending from commercial institutions such as the Saratov Merchant Bank of Arunika (fictional). Coverage would be narrower, but risk-sharing improves.

**Unit U4 Assessment**

We favor Option B, with elements of Option C. Debt sustainability analysis (U4 working paper 24/07) suggests the fund structure keeps debt below our 45% debt-to-GDP anchor even under a stress scenario of 3% currency depreciation and 2% GDP growth shortfall. The tariff surcharge is regressive; we propose compensating transfers of AR 9 billion annually through the Household Energy Credit administered by the Ministry of Social Affairs.

**Risks**

1. Political resistance to the surcharge in the Halvet Highlands, where collection rates fall below 40%.
2. REFF bond issuance may crowd out planned treasury issuance of AR 120 billion in FY2026; sequencing must be coordinated with our auction calendar.
3. Weak RPA accounting standards could delay investment-grade ratings for the fund.

**Recommendations**

1. Approve Option B design; legislate REFF by Q4 2025.
2. Cap sovereign guarantees to RPA at AR 150 billion, declining 10% annually.
3. Direct the Debt Management Office (U4 liaison: Office of Contingent Liabilities) to negotiate risk-sharing terms with the Meridian Regional Development Bank.
4. Reconcile all figures with the Budget Directorate within 30 days.

Unit U4 will circulate Revision 2 following inter-agency comments.

**— End of Memo —**

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U4 (Public Debt Management) — Policy Analysis Memo**
**Subject: Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing — Revision 2**
**Date: 14 March 2025 | For: Hon. Minister, Deputy Minister, Steering Committee on Energy Finance**

**Purpose**

This memo supersedes Revision 1 (8 January 2025). It incorporates audited 2024 disbursement data from the Regional Treasury Office in Kelantar and revised cost projections from the Viremo Basin survey. All figures are U4 estimates.

**Updated Findings**

1. The Rural Electrification Access Fund (REAF) faces a projected shortfall of Arunikan Shillings (AS) 340 million by FY2027, up from AS 210 million estimated in Revision 1. The increase reflects higher connection costs in the Viremo Basin, where average per-household connection costs have risen from AS 1,850 to AS 2,420.

2. Concessional borrowing currently covers 62% of REAF capital. The Northlund Development Facility has signalled a reduction in its annual window from AS 180 million to AS 130 million from FY2026, a sharper cut than assumed in Revision 1.

3. The Ministry of Energy's Tariff Stabilisation Account, which subsidises rural tariffs, is running a monthly deficit of AS 9.5 million against an assumed AS 6 million.

4. Household connection uptake in the Doreth and Savell districts reached 71% in 2024, above the 58% modelled in Revision 1, indicating stronger-than-expected willingness to pay at current tariff levels.

**Assessment**

The revised figures improve the revenue outlook but worsen the financing gap. Stronger uptake supports viability of a blended financing model, yet the shortfall now exceeds U4's prudent borrowing headroom. Issuing sovereign guarantees for the full gap would raise contingent liabilities to an estimated 1.9% of GDP, above U4's recommended ceiling of 1.4%.

**Options**

**Option A — Status quo.** Continue current grants-plus-concessional-loans structure. Projected shortfall persists; risk of service interruptions in Viremo Basin by FY2027. Not recommended.

**Option B — Blended facility with partial risk guarantee.** Combine a scaled concessional window (AS 120 million/year), a new municipally backed bond line via the Kelantar Infrastructure Trust, and U4-issued partial risk guarantees capped at AS 150 million. Estimated contingent liability: 0.9% of GDP. Recommended.

**Option C — Full sovereign borrowing.** Issue AS 400 million in 10-year bonds. Fast but raises debt-service costs by AS 48 million/year and crowds out planned refinancing of the Savell road portfolio.

**Recommendation**

U4 recommends Option B, with safeguards: (i) guarantee cap reviewed annually; (ii) tariff indexation linked to the rural consumer price index from FY2026; (iii) connection subsidies redirected to lowest-income quintiles only, saving an estimated AS 22 million/year.

**Next Steps**

U4 will prepare a draft guarantee framework by 30 April 2025 and consult the Debt Policy Committee and the Office of the Auditor-General before submission to Cabinet in May.

**Prepared by:** Unit U4, Debt Policy and Analysis Division

**MINISTRY OF FINANCE — REPUBLIC OF ARUNIKA**
**Unit U4 (Public Debt Policy)**

**MEMORANDUM — Revision 3**
**Subject: Redesigning Rural Electrification Financing**
**Date: 14 May 2025 | Author: U4 Secretariat | Circulation: Deputy Minister, Debt Management Office**

---

**1. Purpose**

This memo supersedes Revisions 1 and 2 (March and April 2025). It updates the costing and sustainability analysis of the Rural Electrification Programme (REP) with the latest Q1-2025 borrowing data and revised tariff collections from the Eastern Corridor districts.

**2. Problem**

The REP is financed through a mix of sovereign guarantees and direct budget lines, with the Central Power Development Fund (CPDF) acting as intermediary. U4's revised projections show the programme's cost of capital has risen from 9.2% to 11.4% since our last revision, driven by the weakening of the aruni against settlement currencies and two missed interest transfers from the Velloria Provincial Utilities Board. At current disbursement rates, REP-related debt will reach 3.1% of GDP by 2028, up from 2.4% estimated in Revision 2.

**3. Updated Findings**

- **Collection gap widened.** Metered connections in the Kandesi and Olembe districts report tariff recovery of only 58%, versus 63% assumed in Revision 2. The shortfall is projected at ARU 42 billion annually by 2027.
- **Guarantee exposure.** Callable guarantees to the CPDF total ARU 88 billion, of which U4 now classifies ARU 21 billion as high-risk, an increase from ARU 14 billion previously.
- **Maturity profile.** The 2029 bullet repayment on the Solvane Infrastructure Bond coincides with peak REP drawdown, creating an ARU 30 billion refinancing spike.

**4. Proposed Redesign**

U4 recommends shifting from sovereign-led financing to a blended structure:

(a) Convert the CPDF into a ring-fenced special-purpose vehicle with capped state recourse, limiting contingent liability to 40% of its portfolio.

(b) Introduce a volumetric risk-sharing facility with the Regional Development Consortium of Arunika (RDCA), under which private lenders absorb first losses up to ARU 15 billion.

(c) Refinance the Solvane bullet in 2026 through a phased exchange offer, reducing peak exposure by an estimated ARU 12 billion.

(d) Redirect the existing fuel levy surcharge (0.8%) as a dedicated revenue backstop, projected to yield ARU 18 billion per year.

**5. Risks**

The redesign reduces headline debt stress but transfers delivery risk to the RDCA structure. If tariff reform in the Southern Highlands stalls, the backstop revenue could fall short by ARU 6–8 billion. Political economy sensitivities around subsidy removal in Zarnai Province remain a constraint; a phased approach over 18 months is advised.

**6. Recommendation**

U4 requests approval to open negotiations with the RDCA by end-Q2 and to table the Solvane exchange proposal at the June Debt Committee. Revision 4 will follow once Q2 collection data are available.

---
*Prepared by U4 — Public Debt Policy. Figures are preliminary and unaudited.*

text:
**MEMO KEBIJAKAN — REVISI 1**

**Kepada:** Yth. Menteri Keuangan Republik Arunika
**Dari:** Unit Kebijakan Perpajakan (U1)
**Perihal:** Kajian dampak fiskal portofolio utang berdenominasi valuta asing
**Tanggal:** 14 Purnama 4729
**Nomor:** U1/KJ/057-1

**1. Ringkasan**

Sebagaimana mandat U1 atas kebijakan perpajakan, memo ini menilai dampak fiskal portofolio utang negara berdenominasi valuta asing (valas) dari kacamata penerimaan pajak dan risiko anggaran. Kesimpulan utama: konsentrasi utang valas saat ini menciptakan kerentanan fiskal yang secara langsung membebani target penerimaan pajak saat kurs depreciasi, dan kami merekomendasikan penguatan kaitan antara manajemen utang dan proyeksi penerimaan.

**2. Latar dan Angka Kunci**

Berdasarkan data Kantor Statistik Fiskal Kota Laruna, utang berdenominasi valas mencapai 41 persen dari total utang negara, atau setara 18,3 persen PDB, dengan mata uang dominan dua valuta mitra utama. Depresiasi kurs sebesar 7,2 persen tahun lalu menaikkan beban bunga dan amortisasi valas sebesar 3,1 miliar tarik — sekitar 0,4 persen PDB. Realokasi anggaran untuk menutup defisit ini menggerus alokasi subsidi daerah di wilayah Selatan Hemba dan mengancam pencapaian target penerimaan pajak pusat sebesar 2,6 persen.

**3. Dampak terhadap Kebijakan Perpajakan**

Dari sisi U1, ada tiga saluran dampak:

a. **Efect pembayaran bunga lunas pajak.** Bunga atas utang valas yang dibayarkan ke pihak luar negeri tidak masuk basis pajak dalam negeri; setiap kenaikan beban bunga valas mengurangi kesempatan penerimaan PPh lembaga keuangan domestik yang menjadi mitra transaksi. Estimasi kerugian penerimaan: 180 juta tarik per 1 persen depresiasi.

b. **Tekanan pada rabat pajak daerah.** Depresiasi memaksa pemerintah pusat memangkas transfer ke Pemerintah Kota Vandelir dan Pemerintah Provinsi Kirao, yang merespons dengan menaikkan pajak daerah setempat — menciptakan beban efektif gabungan yang tidak terkoordinasi.

c. **Volatilitas proyeksi.** Ketidakpastian kurs menyebabkan penargetan penerimaan yang konservatif berlebihan; margin konservasi kami rata-rata 3,4 persen, melebihi kebutuhan prudensial.

**4. Opsi Kebijakan**

**Opsi A:** Batas paksa 35 persen porsi valas dalam portofolio utang. Pro: mengurangi eksposur; Kontra: premi likuiditas sekitar 40 basis poin.

**Opsi B:** Lindung nilai (lindung nilai) melalui Kantor Manajemen Utang Negeri untuk 50 persen eksposur. Biaya tahunan: 0,3 persen dari nilai terlindung, namun menstabilkan baseline penerimaan pajak.

**Opsi C:** Koordinasi formal antara U1 dan Kantor Manajemen Utang Negeri: skenario kurs dipaksa menjadi input wajib proyeksi penerimaan pajak per semester.

U1 mengusulkan kombinasi Opsi B dan C sebagai jalur paling efisien, dengan catatan bahwa Opsi A perlu dikaji terlebih dahulu oleh unit pengelola utang, di luar kewenangan kami.

**5. Batasan Kajian**

Angka bersifat estimasi U1 berbasis model sederhana; unit pengelola utang dan unit statistik dapat memiliki angka berbeda. Memo ini tidak mewakili posisi Kementerian.

**Disiapkan oleh:** Tim U1, Kantor Cabang Laruna
**Menunggu persetujuan:** Kepala U1

**MEMO KEBIJAKAN — UNIT U1 (Kebijakan Perpajakan)**
**Kementerian Keuangan Republik Arunika**

**Perihal:** Kajian dampak fiskal portofolio utang berdenominasi valuta asing
**Status:** Revisi 2 — memperbarui angka Revisi 1
**Tanggal:** 12 Maret, Tahun Anggaran 2029
**Penyusun:** U1, berdasarkan mandat kebijakan perpajakan

---

**1. Ringkasan**

Revisi ini memperbarui temuan Revisi 1 dengan data fiskal triwulan IV 2028 yang baru dirilis oleh Direktorat Statistik Fiskal Kota Lumen. Kesimpulan utama tidak berubah: porsi utang berdenominasi valuta asing (valas) tetap menjadi sumber risiko fiskal yang signifikan, namun besaran dampaknya lebih tinggi dari estimasi sebelumnya.

**2. Gambaran Portofolio**

Per 31 Desember 2028, utang berdenominasi valas mencapai 1.240 miliar krun (Kr), atau 38% dari total utang negara — naik dari 35% pada estimasi Revisi 1. Komposisi didominasi obligasi jangka menengah 5–10 tahun (62%), diikuti pinjaman bilateral (21%) dan instrumen pasar (17%).

**3. Dampak Fiskal Terkini**

Tiga temuan utama Revisi 2:

a. **Beban bunga.** Proyeksi beban bunga utang valas TA 2029 naik menjadi 96 Kr (sebelumnya 88 Kr Revisi 1), setara 11,2% total belanja negara. Kenaikan disebabkan kenaikan suku acuan Bank Sentral Arunika sebesar 75 basis poin pada bulan lalu.

b. **Efek nilai tukar.** Depresiasi krun terhadap basket valas utang sebesar 6,4% menambah nilai buku utang sebesar 74 Kr. U1 memperkirakan dampak fiskal bersih — setelah memperhitungkan pos penimbang nilai tukar — sebesar 52 Kr, dibanding estimasi 41 Kr dalam Revisi 1.

c. **Rasio utang.** Rasio utang terhadap PDB diproyeksikan mencapai 58,7% (sebelumnya 56,9%), dengan depresiasi menyumbang 1,8 poin persentase.

**4. Implikasi Kebijakan Perpajakan**

Sebagai unit kebijakan perpajakan, U1 menyoroti tiga implikasi:

- **Ketahanan basis pajak.** Beban bunga valas yang naik menekan ruang fiskal untuk insentif pajak investasi. U1 menyarankan penundaan pelongeran pajak korporasi yang direncanakan TA 2030, dengan estimasi penghematan 30 Kr per tahun.

- **Pungutan atas arus modal.** U1 mengevaluasi kenaikan tarif pajak atas bunga yang dibayarkan ke peminjam nonresiden dari 12% ke 15%, berpotensi menambah penerimaan 9–11 Kr per tahun, dengan risiko moderat terhadap arus masuk investasi.

- **Hedging dan perlakuan pajak.** Perlakuan pajak atas kontrak lindung nilai pemerintah perlu diselaraskan dengan Peraturan Bersama No. 7/2028 agar pos penimbang tidak menimbulkan beban pajak ganda pada BUMA penerima mandat hedging di kawasan Pelabuhan Sendrai.

**5. Rekomendasi**

1. Batasi penerbitan obligasi valas baru maksimal 15% dari penerbitan TA 2029.
2. Bentuk kelompok kerja gabungan U1–U4 (Manajemen Utang) untuk sinkronisasi strategi hedging dan perlakuan pajaknya.
3. Kaji ulang tarif pajak bunga nonresiden pada semester pertama TA 2029.

**6. Catatan**

Seluruh angka adalah estimasi U1 dan dapat berbeda dengan proyeksi resmi Biro Perencanaan. Revisi 3 direncanakan setelah rilis data PDB triwulan I 2029.

**Disetujui untuk distribusi internal:**
Kepala Unit U1, Kota Lumen

text:
**MEMO ANALISIS KEBIJAKAN**
**Unit U1 – Kebijakan Perpajakan, Kementerian Keuangan Republik Arunika**
**Perihal: Kajian dampak fiskal portofolio utang berdenominasi valuta asing**
**Status: Revisi 3 – memperbarui angka Revisi 2 (Oktober 1147)**
**Tanggal: 17 Tahun Baru 1148**

**1. Tujuan**
Memo ini memperbarui kajian Revisi 2 mengenai dampak fiskal dari portofolio utang luar negeri pemerintah pusat berdenominasi valuta asing, dengan memperhitungkan data realisasi triwulan terbaru dan proyeksi kurs yang disesuaikan.

**2. Temuan Utama yang Diperbarui**

a. *Saldo dan komposisi.* Saldo utang luar negeri pusat mencapai 1.840 miliar Kupang pada akhir triwulan ketiga 1147 (naik dari 1.710 miliar Kupang pada Revisi 2), setara 31,2% dari total utang pemerintah. Sekitar 68% denominasi adalah Dolar Arden, 22% Franc Lembah, dan 10% mata uang lain.

b. *Beban bunga.* Proyeksi beban bunga utang valas untuk tahun anggaran 1148 naik menjadi 214 miliar Kupang (Revisi 2: 188 miliar), akibat kenaikan suku acuan global dan penetrasi pasar Pinjaman Kota Selatan yang baru dibuka.

c. *Risiko kurs.* Depresiasi Kupang sebesar 6,4% terhadap Dolar Arden sejak Juni menambah beban pembayaran pokok setara 96 miliar Kupang tahun ini, lebih tinggi dari estimasi 71 miliar Kupang pada Revisi 2.

**3. Dampak Fiskal dari Perspektif U1**

a. *Tekanan pada ruang fiskal pajak.* Kenaikan beban bunga menekan surplus utama; untuk mempertahankan target surplus utama 2,1% PDB, kebutuhan penerimaan pajak naik 1,3% di atas proyeksi sebelumnya.

b. *Implikasi kebijakan pajak.* U1 merekomendasikan penguatan kepatuhan di sektor impor Pelabuhan Nirwana (potensi tambahan 28 miliar Kupang) dan peninjauan insentif pajak wilayah ekonomi khusus Tanjung Baja (potensi 15 miliar Kupang), sebagai alternatif utang valas baru.

c. *Efek haircut tidak diperlukan.* Rasio utang valas terhadap PDB (27,9%) masih di bawah ambang kehati-hatian internal 35%; tidak disarankan restrukturasi.

**4. Rekomendasi**
1. Batasi penerbitan baru denomina­si Dolar Arden maksimal 180 miliar Kupang tahun 1148; alihkan ke utang domestik.
2. Aktifkan lindung nilai kurs untuk 40% portofolio melalui Bank Sentral Arunika.
3. Terapkan paket penguatan penerimaan pajak sesuai butir 3b guna melindungi surplus utama.

**5. Catatan**
Angka memakai basis data Triwulan III 1147 dan menggantikan seluruh angka Revisi 2. Koordinasi lanjutan dengan Unit U4 (Manajemen Utang) dijadwalkan pada pertemuan Komite Utang di Gedung Keuangan, Kota Harnata.

**MEMORANDUM ANALISIS KEBIJAKAN**

**Kementerian Keuangan Republik Arunika**
**Unit U2 – Mandat: Anggaran**
**Nomor: U2/KAJIAN/017/Revisi-1**

**Perihal: Kajian dampak fiskal portofolio utang berdenominasi valuta asing**

**A. Latar Belakang**

Sejalan dengan amanat Peraturan Anggaran Negara Tahunan No. 8/AU/2024, Unit U2 melakukan kajian atas portofolio utang luar negeri pemerintah pusat yang berdenominasi valuta asing. Kajian ini merupakan revisi pertama atas memorandum tanggal 12 Agustus 2025, dengan penyelarasan data bersumber dari Direktorat Penataan Portofolio Wilayah Seloagung dan Kantor Rukminata.

**B. Temuan Utama**

1. Total utang berdenominasi valuta asing mencapai 1.240 miliar kruna, atau 34,7% dari portofolio utang nasional. Komposisi terbesar: dolar esmaria (52%), euro eruna (31%), yen nihonara (11%), sisanya mata uang lain.

2. Rata-rata suku bunga kupon portofolio valas adalah 4,2%, lebih tinggi 0,8 poin persentase dibanding utang berdenominasi kruna. Beban bunga tahunan diperkirakan 52,1 miliar kruna, naik dari 47,6 miliar kruna pada anggaran awal.

3. Depresiasi kruna sebesar 6,3% terhadap dolar esmaria sejak awal tahun fiskal menambah kebutuhan anggaran pembayaran utang pokok dan bunga sebesar 18,4 miliar kruna. Ini belum dianggarkan dalam Dokumen Anggaran Pelaksanaan yang diterbitkan Kantor Bendoarlum.

4. Rasio utang valas terhadap penerimaan negara berada di 22,9%, masih di bawah ambang kehati-hatian internal 30%, namun tren menurunnya cadangan devisa tercatat di Layar Pemantauan Triwulan-3 menunjukkan ruang pengelolaan risiko yang menyempit.

**C. Dampak Fiskal**

Kenaikan beban utang valas memperbesar defisit anggaran proyeksi dari 2,8% menjadi 3,1% terhadap produk domestik bruto, melewati batas kebijakan 3,0%. Tanpa tindakan penyesuaian, alokasi belanja pembangunan di sektor irigasi Bendungan Talomerak dan jalan antarwilkota Seroja–Kelumbayan berpotensi dipangkas guna menjaga konsolidasi fiskal.

**D. Opsi Kebijakan**

1. **Opsi A – Penguatan lindung nilai:** Melaksanakan lindung nilai atas 40% dari jatuh tempo valas tahun depan melalui kontrak berjangka dengan Lembaga Bank Pemerkosa Sembilu. Estimasi biaya lindung nilai 3,2 miliar kruna per tahun.

2. **Opsi B – Pergantian mata uang:** Mengurangi penerbitan obligasi dolar esmaria dan beralih ke euro eruna pada dua lelang berikutnya di Bursa Palerukan, memanfaatkan selisih imbal hasil yang lebih rendah 1,1 poin persentase.

3. **Opsi C – Konsolidasi pasif:** Mempertahankan struktur eksisting dan menerima risiko kurs, dengan alokasi cadangan anggaran tambahan 20 miliar kruna.

**E. Rekomendasi U2**

Unit U2 merekomendasikan kombinasi Opsi A dan B secara bertahap, dengan alokasi anggaran tambahan 6,5 miliar kruna pada revisi anggaran semester berikutnya. Opsi C dinilai tidak memadai karena melemahkan kredibilitas konsolidasi fiskal di mata mitra kreditur.

**F. Catatan**

Data kajian bersumber dari basis milik U2 dan dapat berbeda dari publikasi unit lain. Revisi ini mengoreksi angka beban bunga pada versi pertama. Uraian lanjut akan disampaikan dalam rapat komite fiskal triwulanan.

Disusun oleh: Unit U2 — Mandat Anggaran

**1. Latar Belakang**
Revisi 1 memo ini (12 Februari 2026) memperkirakan beban fiskal portofolio utang valuta asing berdasarkan data per Triwulan III 2025. Sejak itu, Direktorat Statistik Keuangan Talur mempublikasikan data Triwulan IV 2025, dan Bank Sentral Padaric merevisi proyeksi kurs. Memo ini memutakhirkan angka-angka utama.

**2. Temuan Terbaru**
Portofolio utang luar negeri pemerintah tercatat ARD 1.240 triliun setara per Desember 2025, naik dari estimasi ARD 1.180 triliun pada Revisi 1, akibat penerbitan sukuk global Seri-K sebesar USD 2,1 miliar di pasar Velnor. Porsi denominasi mata uang asing mencapai 38% dari total utang negara (sebelumnya 35%).

Dampak fiskal utama:
- **Beban bunga**: Proyeksi pembayaran bunga utang VA tahun 2026 naik dari ARD 86 triliun (Revisi 1) menjadi ARD 94 triliun, didorong kenaikan suku bunga acuan di negara kreditur utama dan pelunasan kupon obligasi Seri-K.
- **Sensitivitas kurs**: Berdasarkan model Unit U2, depresiasi kurs RPZ sebesar 5% terhadap dolar Dunara menambah beban pokok utang dalam anggaran sekitar ARD 31 triliun, lebih tinggi dari estimasi ARD 27 triliun sebelumnya.
- **Rasio beban bunga terhadap belanja negara**: diproyeksikan 9,7% (sebelumnya 9,1%), masih di bawah pagu kehati-hatian fiskal 12% sebagaimana diatur Peraturan Menteri Keuangan Arunika Kota Sanderil No. 8/2024.

**3. Implikasi Anggaran**
Pemutakhiran ini menambah kebutuhan belanja bunga sekitar ARD 8 triliun pada RAPBA 2026. Unit U2 menyarankan realokasi dari buffer cadangan fiskal di Kantor Pembendaharaan Grumet sebesar ARD 5 triliun dan efisiensi belanja barang milik negara sebesar ARD 3 triliun, tanpa menambah defisit.

**4. Risiko**
(1) Volatilitas kurs menjelang lelang sukuk Seri-L di pasar Hanteb. (2) Konsentrasi jatuh tempo 2027 sebesar ARD 210 triliun yang 60%-nya berdenominasi VA. (3) Penurunan peringkat kredit jika defisit melebihi 2,9% PDB.

**5. Rekomendasi**
a. Membatasi penerbitan utang VA baru maksimal USD 3 miliar per tahun 2026;
b. Mengaktifkan lindung nilai alami melalui swap mata uang dengan rekening korespondensi di Talur;
c. Menyusun strategi penerbitan berbasis mata uang domestik bersama Unit P4 (Manajemen Utang).

Unit U2 akan mengeluarkan pemutakhiran berikutnya setelah data Triwulan I 2026 tersedia.

— Kepala Unit U2, Kantor Anggaran, Kementerian Keuangan Republik Arunika
